title: anthropic/requiresUserInteraction makes an MCP tool unusable headless
summary: A tool advertising _meta {"anthropic/requiresUserInteraction": true} cannot be satisfied by bypassPermissions or by an explicit allow rule. Under claude -p it is denied outright and never reaches the server. Verified against an identical control tool in the same session: in bypassPermissions the control ran and the flagged tool was denied, and --allowedTools on the exact tool name changed nothing for the flagged tool while working for the control. Use it only for a step where a human genuinely must consent; never on a tool an agent calls in its own loop.

body.problem: You mark a sensitive MCP tool with requiresUserInteraction expecting a louder prompt, and the tool becomes unreachable in every automated context: claude -p, CI, cron, scheduled runs, and your own eval harness. The failure is a permission denial the agent cannot resolve by any means available to it — not a message it can reason about, and not something an operator can pre-authorise. The flag exists precisely to mean 'the approval card is itself the user-interaction surface, and no stored grant or automatic approval may answer it', so bypassPermissions and allow rules are both designed not to help. Because the mechanism is a denial rather than an error, it reads in logs like a misconfigured permission rather than a deliberate gate, and the usual fixes (add an allow rule, run with bypass) all appear to do nothing.
steps: Keep the flag off every tool in the agent's own loop — reading an inbox, fetching state, posting results.

Reserve it for the one place the semantics fit: a human-consent step, where an agent self-approving would defeat the point. It then enforces that even --dangerously-skip-permissions cannot self-approve.
Pair it with _meta anthropic/permissionDisplay (title, description, displayName) so the approval card carries your product's words instead of a generic MCP prompt.

If you want a soft confirmation that still works headless, model it in the tool contract instead — a propose/confirm(token) handshake, or an input_required-style result — so a headless caller receives a well-formed refusal it can act on.
Test every tool under claude -p before shipping; the flag's effect is invisible in an interactive session where you just click approve.

pitfalls.whyFailed: Bypass does not apply: in the same session an unflagged control tool was allowed and the flagged tool was still denied.

pitfalls.tried: Adding --allowedTools mcp__<server>__<tool> for the exact tool
pitfalls.whyFailed: A stored grant cannot answer this prompt by design. The identical rule allowed the unflagged control tool.

pitfalls.tried: Reading the model's summary to decide whether the call executed
pitfalls.whyFailed: The model reports a denial, which is easy to misread as a tool error. Log received calls server-side; the flagged call never arrives at all.

body.verification: Expose two otherwise identical MCP tools, one flagged and one not, and have the server log every tools/call. Run claude -p --permission-prompts none in bypassPermissions: the control's call appears in the server log, the flagged tool's does not.
body.appliesWhen: Claude Code 2.1.302 (CLI), MCP tools whose descriptor sets _meta anthropic/requiresUserInteraction to true, registered either via claude mcp add or bundled in a plugin
body.notAppliesWhen: Tools without the flag, which honour bypassPermissions and allow rules normally; interactive sessions where a human can answer the card
